name: notification
intent: Collect the errors an operation produces into a single result object and return that object to the caller, so every validation or domain failure is reported at once instead of the operation aborting on the first one.
problem: Validation and other expected failure conditions are signalled with exceptions or early returns, so a caller learns about one failure per attempt: a form or remote API user plays whack-a-mole with the input, each round trip reveals only the first complaint, and normal flow is entangled with exception handling for a condition the code fully expects to see.
context: Layered or remotely separated systems where validation belongs to code that must not depend on the presentation, where several independent checks over the same input can fail at once, and where reporting all failures in one response or one pass matters more than aborting early - request validation, batch imports, configuration or protocol parsers, and domain rules evaluated behind a Service Layer.
benefits: Every failure in one round trip: the caller can present or log the complete set of problems instead of revealing one per retry.
Expected failure stays in the normal flow: input the code regularly sees needs no exception type, no handler and no stack unwind.
Diagnostics stay structured: error codes, offending field paths and severities travel as data, so the presentation can localise, highlight and group instead of parsing prose.
The result is plain data and therefore transportable - it serialises into a DTO or an HTTP problem response where an exception object cannot.
Validation stays independent of the presentation (Separated Presentation): the domain hands back a value to interrogate instead of reaching into the UI.
tradeoffs: The caller must actually inspect the result: a forgotten hasErrors check lets invalid data proceed silently, which is the pattern's signature failure mode.

Checks that depend on earlier ones need explicit short-circuit logic inside the accumulation (a policy lookup only makes sense once the policy id parsed), and that conditional wiring is easy to get wrong.
The notification must be threaded through the validation call graph or parked in ambient/session state; the first widens every signature, the second hides data flow and breaks under concurrency.
The accumulator is mutable: a shared or reused instance leaks errors across requests or threads, and concurrent checks need their own instance or a lock.
Errors become a cross-layer contract (codes, field names, severities) that has to be versioned and kept transport-safe - no references to domain objects when the boundary is remote.
Accumulation can waste work and produce noise: running expensive checks after a fatal failure, or returning hundreds of entries for one malformed input, is worse than failing fast.

It must not swallow faults: genuinely unexpected conditions (I/O failure, broken invariant) still belong in exceptions, and returning them as notification entries loses both the stack and the fail-fast guarantee.

participants.responsibility: Mutable accumulator that owns the collected entries, offers an add operation, answers whether any error is present, and exposes the entries for inspection.
One diagnostic entry: a stable code plus the offending field or path, an optional message and severity (error/warning/information), and optionally the rejected value.
Evaluates one independent rule and appends an Error to the notification instead of throwing or returning early; it never decides what the caller should do about the failure.
Creates the notification, runs the checks (short-circuiting the dependent ones), and returns it together with the outcome to the caller.
Interrogates the returned notification, renders or routes every recorded entry, and proceeds with the work only when no error is present.
The shared, versioned set of codes and presentation-side texts that domain and presentation both reference, so messages are not embedded in the domain.

use_cases: HTTP or form request validation where a single response must show every invalid field.
Remote validation: a client submits a DTO to a service layer and pays a network round trip per attempt, so batching all failures matters.
Batch import, migration or ETL jobs that must report per-row diagnostics (with their offending fields) while continuing with the remaining rows.
Configuration, protocol or DSL parsers that diagnose as many syntax and semantic problems as possible in one pass.
Domain rule evaluation behind a Service Layer that returns a transportable result to a remote facade instead of letting domain exceptions cross the wire.
Editor- or compiler-like tooling that reports every diagnostic for a document instead of stopping at the first error.
Rails ActiveModel::Validations with ActiveModel::Errors collects multiple attribute-level errors (including codes and paths) before a form or API response is rendered.
Symfony Validator returns a ConstraintViolationList for object, scalar or array validation, allowing a boundary to map every violation rather than only the first.
Pydantic model validation exposes a structured list through ValidationError.errors(), so an API can report multiple field locations and error types together.
avoid_when: The failure is genuinely unexpected (I/O outage, corrupted invariant, programming error): throw or panic and fail fast - the notification is for outcomes the code expects to see.
Only one thing can fail, or the caller aborts immediately anyway: a boolean, an error code or a Result is simpler than an accumulator.
The checks are strictly dependent, so only the first failure is meaningful: a guard clause expresses that ordering directly.

A framework or validator already returns the aggregate (Bean Validation violations, DataAnnotations results, schema validators, Vapor Validations): do not hand-roll a parallel notification type next to it.
The value must be valid at all times (an aggregate invariant): validate in the constructor or factory and throw, then let the notification govern only boundary input.
The errors would only ever be logged: log at the point of detection and keep the return contract simple.
anti_patterns: Returning a notification that the caller is free to ignore (or that the API makes optional), so validation becomes decorative and invalid data proceeds.
Using the notification for exceptional faults - I/O errors, contract violations, caught-and-swallowed exceptions - which lose their stack trace and fail-fast guarantee.
A global or static notification instance reused across requests or threads, so errors from one interaction show up in another.
Free-form message strings without codes or field paths, forcing the caller to parse prose and making the error surface impossible to localise or test.
Accumulating errors and then running the dependent work anyway (registering a claim whose policy id was never resolved).
Two parallel error channels - throwing for some checks and accumulating others - with no documented rule for which is which.
design_principles: Expected failure belongs to the normal flow; exceptions are reserved for genuinely unexpected events (the rule Fowler quotes from the Pragmatic Programmers).
Separated presentation: the domain returns data that describes the failures; it neither depends on nor talks to the presentation.
Single responsibility: diagnosing input and deciding what to do about the diagnosis are separate concerns, and the notification carries only the diagnosis.
Explicit interface: error codes, field paths and severities make the failure surface part of the contract instead of an implementation detail of message strings.
Keep invariants where they belong: objects that must never be invalid still validate at construction and throw; the notification governs boundary input, not internal consistency.
best_practices: Make the result impossible to ignore: return the notification (optionally inside a Result/Response type) instead of filling a caller-supplied out-parameter.
Separate errors from warnings and information, and record a severity per entry so the caller can decide what blocks the operation.
Identify each entry by a stable code plus the offending field or path; keep human-readable text out of the domain and resolve it in the presentation.
Create one notification per operation; never share a mutable instance across requests or threads.
Short-circuit dependent checks explicitly and document the ordering they require.
Bound the result: deduplicate and cap the entries so pathological input cannot produce unbounded diagnostics.
Keep the entries transport-safe (serialisable data only) whenever the notification crosses a process boundary.
Carry the notification consistently (for example on a shared DTO layer supertype) when many interactions need it, rather than threading it ad hoc through each signature.
sources: Fowler, M., Notification (eaaDev, 9 August 2004) - defines the pattern: an object that collects information about errors in the domain layer and communicates it to the presentation, with error codes, warnings, transport safety and the Layer Supertype variant.

Fowler, M., Replacing Throwing Exceptions with Notification in Validations (9 December 2014) - the refactoring that replaces fail-fast validation throws with an accumulated notification; source of the expected-vs-exceptional rule and the caveat that dependent checks need conditional logic.
Fowler, M., Notification (DSL Catalog) - concise catalog definition of the Notification pattern as accumulating validation errors rather than failing fast.
Rails Active Model Errors API - ActiveModel::Errors collects and manages multiple validation errors, including attribute paths and error types.
Symfony Validator documentation - validate() returns a ConstraintViolationList containing the violations from object or value validation.
Pydantic Validation documentation - ValidationError exposes structured details for multiple failures, including type, location, message and input.
Software Engineering Stack Exchange discussion on replacing throwing exceptions with Notification in validations - cautionary discussion of when aggregate validation or alternatives fit better.
